lines.en: What distinguishes a professional email from a casual one is not length, but the clarity of what happens next.
It is better to deliver bad news plainly and early than to wrap it in hopeful language until it is too late.
Were every meeting to end with a decision and a name, half the meetings would disappear.
However urgent your message may feel to you, to the reader it is one of a hundred.
Not until you have written 'I was wrong' to a client do you understand the value of writing it well.
It is advised that all feedback be specific, actionable, and kind; two out of three is not enough.
What the promotion announcement did not mention was who would do his old job.
The minutes of the meeting, though brief, managed to offend three departments in two sentences.
Little is achieved by copying the whole company on a complaint except theatre.
Rarely has anyone been promoted for a beautifully formatted spreadsheet alone.
What the apology email achieved in three sentences, three meetings had failed to repair.
It is a mark of seniority to write briefly; only the insecure feel the need to fill the page.
Were every reply-all to require a ten-second pause, office traffic would drop by half.
Not until the report was rewritten for the reader, not the writer, did anyone actually read it.
However routine the message, its tone will be remembered long after its content is forgotten.
